class="c-article-section__figure-description" data-test="bottom-caption" id="figure-7-desc"><p>Subclusters and pseudotime analysis of the malignant basal cells in LUSC. <b>a</b> UMAP of 8016 malignant basal cells from LUSC, colored with different clusters, and the fraction of different stages of each cluster were labeled with a pie chart. <b>b</b> Diffusion map of malignant basal cells from LUSC, colored with different stages. The diffusion map colored with pseudotime was plotted at the left top corner. <b>c</b> Density of pseudotime colored with different stages. <b>d</b> Dot plot of the mean level of expression (dot intensity, blue scale) of cluster makers and indicated basal cell markers and percent of cells in population with detected expression (dot size). Generic markers colored in green, proliferation basal (Bas-p) markers colored in red, proximal basal (Bas-px) markers colored in yellow and differentiating basal (Bas-d) markers colored in blue. <b>e</b> UMAP plot showed the log2 transformed stemness score calculated using the mean level of expression of Bas-p markers. <b>f</b> Heatmap showed the cluster scores of all non-cycling cells (left) and cycling cells (right). Within each group, the cells were defined by maximal score, for cells mapping to one cluster. <b>g</b> The expression of <i>KPNA2</i> in LUSC. Immunofluorescence staining indicated the location of <i>KPNA2</i> level in lung cancer cells (green), CK5/6 (Cytokeratin 5/6) was used as the marker of lung squamous carcinoma cells (red), <i>KRT5</i> (Keratin 5) was used as the marker of basal cells in normal lung, the cell nucleus was co-stained with DAPI (blue); Scale bar, 50 μm</p></div></div></figure></div><p>To understand the biological properties of each cluster, we compared our cluster-specific genes (Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#Fig7">7d</a>, Supplementary Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="supplementary material anchor" href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#MOESM1">7a</a>, and Supplementary Table <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="supplementary material anchor" href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#MOESM1">8</a>) to those from a human lung cell atlas.<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 11" title="Travaglini, K. J. et al. A molecular cell atlas of the human lung from single-cell RNA sequencing. Nature 587, 619–625 (2020)." href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#ref-CR11" id="ref-link-section-d86200692e2080">11</a></sup> The basal general markers were broadly expressed in all clusters, while the markers of proximal basal (Bas-px) were highly expressed in cluster 7, and those of differentiating basal (Bas-d) were selectively expressed in cluster 3 (Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#Fig7">7d</a>). Notably, cluster 4 selectively expressed markers from proliferating basal (Bas-p), including <i>MKI67, TOP2A, PBK,</i> and <i>GTSE1</i>. We further utilized the stemness and cell cycling scores and revealed that cluster 4 had the highest stemness score and was mainly classified as cycling cells (Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#Fig7">7e, f</a>), indicating this cluster might have the characteristics of proliferating cells.</p><p>Finally, we experimentally investigated the cluster-specific <i>KPNA2</i> (karyopherin alpha 2) for cluster 4 and <i>PPT1</i> for cluster 7 (described in Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#Fig5">5</a> as stage-I-specific gene). Increased expression of KPNA2 protein was observed in tumor tissues by immunofluorescence staining in comparison to normal lung tissues (Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#Fig7">7g</a>). Overexpression of <i>KPNA2</i> revealed its tumor-promotion role by increasing proliferation (<i>P</i> = 1.02e − 4, <i>t</i> test) (Supplementary Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="supplementary material anchor" href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#MOESM1">7b</a>), migration and invasion of lung cancer H1299 cells (Supplementary Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="supplementary material anchor" href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#MOESM1">7c, d</a>). Taken together, our results revealed clusters of malignant cells that resembled normal lung cell subclusters and a cluster (cluster 4) was with stem-like proliferating features in malignant basal cells, and its maker <i>KPNA2</i> might promote tumor proliferation in LUSC.</p></div></div></section><section data-title="Discussion"><div class="c-article-section" id="Sec10-section"><h2 class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item" id="Sec10">Discussion</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Sec10-content"><p>Inter and intratumor heterogeneity is a key factor contributing to poor prognosis and variation of therapy applications between LUAD and LUSC. The single-cell analysis represents a viable strategy to investigate heterogeneity and characterize recurrent cellular compositions, as well as tumor subtype- and stage-specific transcriptomic landscapes. However, extensive comparisons of heterogeneity in LUAD and LUSC are still limited, which is critical for precision therapy of lung cancer. Here, we performed scRNA-seq and multi-omics profiling of lung cancer from multiple LUAD and LUSC patients. To facilitate the community to use our dataset, we further built a website (<a href="http://lungcancer.chenlulab.com">http://lungcancer.chenlulab.com</a>) providing interactive query gene expression, clustering of all the cell types and data downloads (Supplementary Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="supplementary material anchor" href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#MOESM1">7e</a>).</p><p>CNVs were one of the sources in driving tumor progression and acquiring therapeutic resistance.<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 37" title="Jamal-Hanjani, M. et al. Tracking the evolution of non-small-cell lung cancer. N. Engl. J. Med. 376, 2109–2121 (2017)." href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#ref-CR37" id="ref-link-section-d86200692e2153">37</a></sup> Based on the inferred CNVs, malignant AT2 cells and basal cells from LUAD and LUSC could be divided into multiple subclones. Amplification of <i>EGF</i>R in LUAD and <i>MET</i> in LUSC were unevenly distributed in these subclones. While how the clinical implication of these copy-number alterations in malignant cells remained to be further explored, our single-cell CNVs profiles suggest that different subclones may have different responses to targeting treatment.</p><p>We further developed a deconvolution method for bulk RNA from large cohorts and found recurrent cellular compositions from both scRNA-seq and deconvoluted bulk RNA-seq. Importantly, we revealed that high percentages of Fib and AT2 contributed to poor survival of LUAD and LUSC, suggesting the potential roles of cellular compositions in predicting poor prognosis of lung cancer.</p><p>Our study included samples from tumor and adjacent tissues of patients from different tumor stages. Based on genes identified from the malignant-, stage-, and sub-cluster analyses, we experimentally demonstrated that some genes may play functional roles in tumor progression. Our results consistently highlighted the importance of AT2 cells in LUAD, and their subclusters showed proliferating and differentiating properties.AT2 cells, playing pivotal secretory and regenerative roles to maintain the homeostasis in the alveolus of the lung, are known to be a heterogeneous population and maybe the cells of origin of LUAD.<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 38" title="Parimon, T., Yao, C., Stripp, B. R., Noble, P. W. & Chen, P. Alveolar epithelial type II cells as drivers of lung fibrosis in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Int. J. Mol. Sci. 21, 2269 (2020)." href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#ref-CR38" id="ref-link-section-d86200692e2169">38</a></sup> Experimentally, this hypothesis is supported by immunofluorescence staining and overexpression experiments in H1299 cells, linking eight candidate genes (<i>AQP5</i>, <i>ATF3</i>, <i>AZGP1</i>, <i>ANXA2</i>, <i>CHI3L1</i>, <i>EEF1A2</i>, <i>SPINK1</i>, and <i>S100A13</i>) to their promoting roles in LUAD. Indeed, high expression of <i>AZGP1</i> was reported in multiple malignancy tumors such as lung cancer and breast cancer, which played a vital role in lipid mobilization and contributed to malignancy-associated cachexia.<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 39" title="Albertus, D. L. et al. AZGP1 autoantibody predicts survival and histone deacetylase inhibitors increase expression in lung adenocarcinoma. J. Thorac. Oncol. 3, 1236–1244 (2008)." href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#ref-CR39" id="ref-link-section-d86200692e2201">39</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 40" title="Parris, T. Z. et al. Clinical implications of gene dosage and gene expression patterns in diploid breast carcinoma. Clin. Cancer Res. 16, 3860–3874 (2010)." href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#ref-CR40" id="ref-link-section-d86200692e2204">40</a></sup> And <i>S100A13</i>, a member of the S100 family, was closely associated with aggressive invasive phenotype and angiogenesis.<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 30" title="Pierce, A. et al. Identification of a novel, functional role for S100A13 in invasive lung cancer cell lines. Eur. J. Cancer 44, 151–159 (2008)." href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#ref-CR30" id="ref-link-section-d86200692e2212">30</a></sup> Functioning in delivering aminoacylate-tRNA to a site of the ribosome for decoding of mRNA, <i>EEF1A2</i> played an important role in translation and might also act as an oncogene in lung cancer and pancreatic cancer.<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 41" title="Abbas, W., Kumar, A. & Herbein, G. The eEF1A proteins: at the crossroads of oncogenesis, apoptosis, and viral infections. Front. Oncol. 5, 75 (2015)." href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#ref-CR41" id="ref-link-section-d86200692e2219">41</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 42" title="Liu, S. et al. METTL13 methylation of eEF1A increases translational output to promote tumorigenesis. Cell 176, 491–504 e421 (2019)." href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#ref-CR42" id="ref-link-section-d86200692e2222">42</a></sup></p><p>In LUSC, some subclusters of malignant basal cells showed proliferating features. Their marker genes included <i>PPT1</i> and <i>KPNA2. PPT1</i> was reported as a molecular target of chloroquine derivates in melanoma cell lines, closely correlating with the poor prognosis in several cancers, such as breast cancer, clear cell renal cell carcinoma, head and neck squamous carcinoma, thyroid cancer, and colon adenocarcinoma.<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" title="Rebecca, V. W. et al. A unified approach to targeting the lysosome’s degradative and growth signaling roles. Cancer Discov. 7, 1266–1283 (2017)." href="#ref-CR43" id="ref-link-section-d86200692e2235">43</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" title="Rebecca, V. W. et al. PPT1 promotes tumor growth and is the molecular target of chloroquine derivatives in cancer. Cancer Discov. 9, 220–229 (2019)." href="#ref-CR44" id="ref-link-section-d86200692e2235_1">44</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 45" title="Sharma, G. et al. PPT1 inhibition enhances the antitumor activity of anti-PD-1 antibody in melanoma. JCI Insight 5, e133225 (2020)." href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#ref-CR45" id="ref-link-section-d86200692e2238">45</a></sup> <i>KPNA2</i>, a nucleocytoplasmic transporter known to be involved in many cellular processes including differentiation, development, and immune response<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 46" title="Christiansen, A. & Dyrskjot, L. The functional role of the novel biomarker karyopherin alpha 2 (KPNA2) in cancer. Cancer Lett. 331, 18–23 (2013)." href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#ref-CR46" id="ref-link-section-d86200692e2245">46</a></sup> was also revealed to have the potential act as a stemness marker in LUSC. Overexpression of <i>KPNA2</i> was previously reported in LUAD tissues and negatively regulated by a novel transcription factor interferon regulatory factor-1 (IRF1).<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 47" title="Huang, J. X., Wu, Y. C., Cheng, Y. Y., Wang, C. L. & Yu, C. J. IRF1 negatively regulates oncogenic KPNA2 expression under growth stimulation and hypoxia in lung cancer cells. Onco Targets Ther. 12, 11475–11486 (2019)." href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#ref-CR47" id="ref-link-section-d86200692e2253">47</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 48" title="Fu, F. et al. Development and validation of a five-gene model to predict postoperative brain metastasis in operable lung adenocarcinoma. Int. J. Cancer 147, 584–592 (2020)." href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#ref-CR48" id="ref-link-section-d86200692e2256">48</a></sup> Our study revealed that <i>KPNA2</i> may be a proliferating marker and promote tumor progression in LUSC.</p><p>Notably, our study revealed distinct stemness-related subclusters in both LUAD (cluster 1 in AT2 cells) and LUSC (cluster 4 in basal cells). Cancer stem cells (CSCs) have been referred as “tumor-initiating cells” or “sphere-forming cells”, which promoted tumor progression by increasing tumor proliferation and angiogenesis.<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 49" title="Valent, P. et al. Cancer stem cell definitions and terminology: the devil is in the details. Nat. Rev. Cancer 12, 767–775 (2012)." href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#ref-CR49" id="ref-link-section-d86200692e2266">49</a></sup> Multiple pathways, including Hedgehog, Notch, Nanog, Wnt and PI3K/AKT, are involved in CSCs-mediated tumor promotion.<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 50" title="Lathia, J. D. & Liu, H. Overview of cancer stem cells and stemness for community oncologists. Target Oncol. 12, 387–399 (2017)." href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#ref-CR50" id="ref-link-section-d86200692e2270">50</a></sup> Thus, CSCs are considered as therapy target and yield an improved therapeutic window.<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 51" title="Saygin, C., Matei, D., Majeti, R., Reizes, O. & Lathia, J. D. Targeting cancer stemness in the clinic: from hype to hope. Cell Stem Cell 24, 25–40 (2019)." href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#ref-CR51" id="ref-link-section-d86200692e2274">51</a></sup> Blocking CSCs-related signaling pathways provides promising strategy in tumor therapy, in a cohort of 40 glioblastoma patients who received vismodegib treatment (targeting Hedgehog pathway) for 7 days showed dramatically reduction of ex vivo CD133 + neutrosphere formation.<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 52" title="Sloan, A. E. et al. Targeting glioma-initiating cells in GBM: ABTC-0904, a randomized phase 0/II study targeting the Sonic Hedgehog-signaling pathway. J. Clin. Oncol. 32, 2026–2026 (2014)." href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#ref-CR52" id="ref-link-section-d86200692e2278">52</a></sup> In a 30 breast cancer patients with locally advanced and metastasis, Notch pathway inhibitor MK-0752 induced 11 patients had complete remission and 9 patients achieved stable disease.<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 53" title="Schott, A. F. et al. Preclinical and clinical studies of gamma secretase inhibitors with docetaxel on human breast tumors. Clin. Cancer Res. 19, 1512–1524 (2013)." href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#ref-CR53" id="ref-link-section-d86200692e2282">53</a></sup> Besides signaling pathways, other CSCs-related targets involved surface marker,<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 54" title="Vey, N. et al. Phase I clinical study of RG7356, an anti-CD44 humanized antibody, in patients with acute myeloid leukemia. Oncotarget 7, 32532–32542 (2016)." href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#ref-CR54" id="ref-link-section-d86200692e2287">54</a></sup> CSC microenvironment<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 55" title="Schepers, K., Campbell, T. B. & Passegue, E. Normal and leukemic stem cell niches: insights and therapeutic opportunities. Cell Stem Cell 16, 254–267 (2015)." href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#ref-CR55" id="ref-link-section-d86200692e2291">55</a></sup> and aberrant metabolism.<sup><a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 56" title="Jones, C. L. et al. Inhibition of amino acid metabolism selectively targets human leukemia stem cells. Cancer Cell 34, 724–740 e724 (2018)." href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#ref-CR56" id="ref-link-section-d86200692e2295">56</a></sup> Our results revealed two stemness-like clusters in AT2 and basal cells, which could act as potential candidate targets in future precision lung cancer treatment.</p><p>In summary, our study integrated multi-omics analysis to establish a lung tumor atlas and extensively investigated the heterogeneity variation between LUAD and LUSC, which could be used as a valuable resource for understanding the unique mechanism of tumor progression in lung cancer subtypes, providing a blueprint for potential early-stage diagnosis and treatment for lung cancer.</p></div></div></section>

<p>Inter and intratumor heterogeneity is a key factor contributing to poor prognosis and variation of therapy applications between LUAD and LUSC. The single-cell analysis represents a viable strategy to investigate heterogeneity and characterize recurrent cellular compositions, as well as tumor subtype- and stage-specific transcriptomic landscapes. However, extensive comparisons of heterogeneity in LUAD and LUSC are still limited, which is critical for precision therapy of lung cancer. Here, we performed scRNA-seq and multi-omics profiling of lung cancer from multiple LUAD and LUSC patients. To facilitate the community to use our dataset, we further built a website (<a href="http://lungcancer.chenlulab.com">http://lungcancer.chenlulab.com</a>) providing interactive query gene expression, clustering of all the cell types and data downloads (Supplementary Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="supplementary material anchor" href="/articles/s41392-021-00824-9#MOESM1">7e</a>).</p>

Its metadata includes original sample, tumor subtype, and published cell annotations, and the first benchmark barcode matches the source exactly after the benchmark’s sample-prefix renaming. I’m staging that unchanged metadata into the same Galaxy history and will validate a one-to-one barcode-based sample mapping before using any labels.

The job did produce its mapping table before stopping, so I’m inspecting those overlap margins now to determine whether the source match remains decisive or whether the analysis must revert to de novo annotation.

item.text: The corrected diagnostic is decisive: all 164,616 benchmark rows matched source annotations, and each of the five named candidates had 100% overlap with its source sample. Among them, only Patient_018 and Patient_040 are LUSC. I’m now computing the requested result plus sensitivity rows for the only plausible ambiguity—whether “malignant basal” means LUSC basal cells restricted to tumor tissue or all LUSC basal cells—so the required nearest-20% answer is checked for robustness.

The final Galaxy analysis has completed the exact cell-level joins and is finishing output verification. It checks the full annotated row count against 164,616, calculates dendritic-cell proportions only among the LUSC candidates, and reports the basal-cell percentage under three denominator/tissue conventions to confirm whether rounding changes.
